summary_for_principal:
You asked a fair, sharp question: had I actually run the last piece of work, not just checked its shape. I hadn't — I had only validated it, which checks structure, not behaviour. I ran it now.

Running it found a real problem, not where I expected. My translation followed this system's own instructions literally, exactly where they show how to call another process. Those instructions are wrong: the example syntax silently does nothing, confirmed by testing it directly, separate from my own work. Anyone following the documentation as written would hit the same silent failure.

Fixed both: my own files, and the documentation, so the next person doesn't repeat this. Verified by running the fixed version three ways, including genuinely nested behaviour two steps deep.

One smaller gap noticed, not fixed: a failure inside a called process can sometimes be reported as success. Worth a look, not urgent.

Full test suite: 412 passed, 3 new.

Numbered actions:
1. Nothing needs deciding now — complete and verified.
2. Say if you'd like the smaller masked-failure gap looked at next.

decisions.headline: D39 — spec §9.1's own worked example is corrected: mechanism.inputs: { brief: brief } (bare, unqualified) becomes { brief: state.brief } (fully qualified) — confirmed, by actually running it, that the bare form silently resolves to nothing against the real engine.
decisions.problem: mechanism.inputs' values are resolved via _first_present directly against the calling process's own run_state (inputs.*/state.*/host.*/steps.*) — the same four namespaces every other path in this format uses. A bare, unqualified name matches none of them and always resolves to None. The calling STEP's own in: mapping is never consulted for a PROCESS-mechanism dispatch at all, so there is no third namespace a bare name could mean either. Spec §9.1's own worked example is the only place in the entire document, and the only place in the real corpus, that a bare name is used.
options_rejected: Change the engine so a bare mechanism.inputs name resolves against the calling STEP's own in:-mapped Tool inputs (the more natural reading of §9.1's own apparent intent): rejected for this pass — needs new resolution machinery in the core §9 call mechanism every process-call in the corpus goes through, and the currently-built qualified-path behaviour is deliberate and already tested (tests/engine/test_run.py), not an oversight.
decisions.cost_to_change: Low — a documentation and two-Tool-file correction with no schema, model, or engine behaviour change; reverting restores the literal (non-functional) example text.

evidence.claim: The bare-name form (mechanism.inputs: { brief: brief }) resolves to child_inputs = {'brief': None}, causing the child process's own first input-dependent step to fail with INPUT_UNRESOLVED, absorbed into a FAILED ending, then reported as SUCCESS by a calling step whose own controls (empty, in the minimal reproduction) never caught it.
evidence.source: A minimal, standalone two-node wrapper process (not part of this translation's own files) built directly against grounded-inquiry@1.0.0 with the spec's literal syntax, driven through next() this session — reproduced the identical failure shape outside this translation entirely.

evidence.claim: The qualified-path form (mechanism.inputs: { brief: state.brief }) resolves correctly: the same call reaches grounded-inquiry's own real 'gather' hand-off, and that hand-off can be resumed (twice, through 'gather' then 'interrogate') via report() targeting the nested scope's own path (root/dispatch-grounded-inquiry).
evidence.source: tests/examples/test_recursive_refinement.py::test_a_complex_node_dispatches_the_real_grounded_inquiry_process_and_resumes_its_hand_off, passing after the fix; failing (ENDED/FAILED at the first hop) before it, confirmed test-first.

evidence.claim: The CLEAR and COMPLICATED paths (which never call a PROCESS-mechanism Tool) were unaffected by this bug and unaffected by this fix — re-run before and after, identical results both times.

untouched.location: engine/run.py (_advance_process_call / report()'s own check_controls call for a PROCESS-mechanism STEP)
untouched.divergence: A PROCESS-mechanism call whose child ends FAILED (or another non-success ending) can be reported as the calling STEP's own SUCCESS if the calling Tool declares no controls (or controls that happen to pass regardless), because control-checking runs against the Tool's OWN mapped output shape, not against whether the child's own ending was a 'good' one — result.endings mapping the ending into an output field is the only signal available, and nothing forces the calling process's own route to check it.
untouched.why_not_now: Found as a side effect of chasing D39, not this pass's own scope; fixing it well needs a considered design (should the engine itself refuse an unrouted non-success ending value, or is checking result.outputs.ending entirely the calling process author's own responsibility, as recursive-refinement.process.yaml's own route-inquiry-outcome ROUTE already does correctly?) rather than a reactive patch alongside an unrelated fix.

lessons.maxim: Validating a definition (schema + rule conformance) and running it (real engine behaviour) are different claims, and only the second one is evidence that something works — a translation that 'validates cleanly' can still fail its very first real dispatch if the thing it validated against (here, the spec's own worked example) was itself never executed either.
lessons.incident: examples/recursive-refinement/ passed 17 validate()-based tests and was reported as complete; the principal asked directly whether it had actually been run, and it had not. Running it immediately found a real, previously-unknown bug — not in the translation's own design, but in the spec's own flagship worked example for the exact mechanism (calling another process) the translation most needed to prove.
lessons.destination: tests/examples/test_recursive_refinement.py now carries real engine-execution tests alongside the validate()-only ones, for this file and as a pattern for any future translation.
lessons.proposed_check: When a deliverable's own value depends on it actually running (not just being well-formed), drive it through the real execution path before reporting it complete — 'validates cleanly' is not the same claim as 'works', and should not be presented as though it were.
